title: Merge Many Sorted Lists
statement:
You get an array lists of k singly linked lists. Each list is sorted in non-decreasing order. Combine all of them into one sorted list and return its head.

Some lists may be empty, and lists itself may be empty. Equal values may come in any order.

Lists are written as arrays, so [[1, 4], [2]] means two lists, 1 → 4 and 2. An empty result is null (shown as []).

examples.why: The next value can come from any list at any moment: 1 from the second, 3 from the first, then both 4s from the third.
Empty lists contribute nothing and must not crash the merge.
No lists at all gives an empty result.

constraints: Each list is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Merging two sorted lists is easy. If you merge the lists one after another into a growing result, how many times is an early node walked over?
At each step the next node of the answer is the smallest among the k current fronts. Which data structure gives you the smallest of k items quickly, and lets you replace it?

Put the head of every non-empty list into a min-heap. Pop the smallest, attach it, and push its next node if there is one. Alternatively, merge the lists in pairs, then the results in pairs, like merge sort.

explain.intuition:
With two lists, you compare two fronts. With k lists, the next node of the answer is the smallest of k fronts. Scanning all k fronts for every node costs O(k) per node. A min-heap keeps the k fronts ordered so that taking the smallest and putting its successor back costs only O(log k). Think of k sorted API pages being combined into one feed, always showing the newest item among the pages' heads.

The other good approach is divide and conquer. Merging the lists one by one into a growing result is slow, because the first list's nodes get walked k times. Merging in pairs instead (list 0 with 1, 2 with 3, …, then the results in pairs) means every node takes part in only about log k merges, the same structure as merge sort.
steps: Push the head of every non-empty list into a min-heap ordered by val.
Create a dummy node and a tail pointer.
While the heap is not empty: pop the smallest node, attach it to tail, and move tail.
If that node has a next, push it into the heap.
pitfalls: Pushing null heads into the heap: empty lists in the input crash the comparison.
In Python, pushing (val, node) tuples. On equal values Python then compares the nodes and throws; add a unique counter as a tie-breaker.
Merging into one growing result list one list at a time. It is correct but costs O(k · N), which times out with many small lists.

complexity.time: O(N log k), where N is the total number of nodes

solutions.title: Merge into the result one list at a time
solutions.idea: Keep a result list and merge each input list into it with the two-list merge. The result grows, so early nodes are walked again for every later list.

solutions.title: Min-heap of list fronts
solutions.idea: Keep the current front of every list in a min-heap. Pop the smallest, attach it, push its successor.

solutions.title: Merge in pairs (divide and conquer)
solutions.idea: Merge lists 0+1, 2+3, …, then merge those results in pairs, until one list is left. Each node takes part in about log k merges.
solutions.space: O(1) besides the list of lists

followups: The lists are streams too large for memory, read one node at a time. Which of the two fast approaches still works?
Return only the first m values of the merged result. Can you stop early, and what does that cost?
